title: Dynamic Programming
html:
Dynamic Programming

Solving a problem by solving smaller versions of it and not solving any of them twice. That is the whole idea; the difficulty is entirely in framing.

When it applies

Two properties, both required:

Optimal substructure - the best answer is built from best answers to subproblems. True of shortest paths, false of longest simple paths.

Overlapping subproblems - the same subproblem recurs. This is what separates DP from divide and conquer: mergesort's halves never overlap, so caching buys nothing.

The shape of the work

  1. Define the state. What arguments fully describe a subproblem? Get this wrong and nothing else works.
  2. Write the recurrence. How does one state combine its smaller states?
  3. Identify base cases. The states with no dependencies.
  4. Choose a direction. Top-down with a cache, or bottom-up filling a table.
  5. Reduce space if it pays. Often a row or two is enough.

Step one is where the effort belongs. Once the state is right the recurrence usually follows in a line or two; when the recurrence resists, the state is normally missing a dimension.

Top-down or bottom-up

Top-down (memoisation) - write the natural recursion, cache results. Closer to how you think, and it only computes states actually reachable. Costs stack depth.

Bottom-up (tabulation) - iterate states in dependency order. No recursion, easier to shrink the space, but you must know the order, and it may compute states nothing needs.

Same complexity. Start top-down to find the recurrence, convert if space or stack depth demands.

The recurring families

Linear over one sequence. Answer at i from a few earlier positions. Climbing steps, house-robber, longest increasing subsequence. Often O(1) space after reduction.

Two sequences. A 2-D table indexed by a position in each. Edit distance, longest common subsequence. The three moves - match, skip left, skip right - cover the whole space.

Knapsack. Item index plus remaining capacity. Note the difference: 0/1 knapsack iterates capacity downward so each item is used once; unbounded iterates upward so it can repeat. Same loop, opposite direction, different problem.

Intervals. A table over ranges, growing by length. Matrix-chain ordering, palindromic substrings, burst-balloons.

Over subsets. State is a bitmask of which elements are used. Exponential but tractable to about twenty elements.

Reconstructing the answer

A DP table gives the optimal value. Recovering the actual choices means either storing a decision per state, or walking the table backwards asking which predecessor produced this value. Decide which you need before building the table - retrofitting is painful.

Common mistakes

  • A state that does not capture everything the answer depends on. Symptom: a recurrence that is nearly right.
  • Base cases that are wrong or missing, so the whole table is shifted.
  • Iterating bottom-up in an order where a dependency is not yet computed.
  • Reducing space before the recurrence is verified, and losing a row that was still needed.
  • Reaching for DP where greedy is provably correct, or greedy where it is not.
